lessons.title: Inspection work in the real workplace
lessons.html:
What this work experience module covers

In this module you apply inspection knowledge and skills on real work sites under the guidance of a workplace mentor or supervisor. You will take part in, and progressively lead, inspections at different types of sites. Typical sites for a pest management officer in an agricultural setting include grain silos and bin complexes, feed mills, packhouses, farm stores and homesteads, dairies and piggeries, food factories and warehouses.

Typical inspection activities

  • Preparing for visits: reviewing job requests, site history and trap data.
  • Accessing sites: signing in, induction, confirming scope with the site contact.
  • Carrying out exterior and interior inspections along a systematic route.
  • Servicing monitoring devices and recording counts.
  • Collecting and labelling specimens.
  • Recording findings on site plans and checklists, with photographs.
  • Briefing the client before leaving and writing the inspection report.

Working across different sites

Each type of site teaches different lessons. At a silo complex you learn to inspect bin tops, tunnels, elevator boots and spillage points, and to respect engulfment and fumigant hazards. In a feed mill you learn about dust, conveyors and hidden residues in equipment. On a farm you inspect stores, kraals, sheds and homesteads, and meet rodents, flies, birds, termites and invader plants all on one property. In a food factory you learn strict hygiene rules and audit-ready reporting.

Scenario

Your mentor asks you to inspect a farm grain store before the new maize harvest is brought in. You find old maize in the corners, live flour beetles in floor cracks, rat droppings along one wall, a gap under the roller door and a leaking gutter. You record each finding on the site plan, photograph it, and recommend cleaning, proofing, gutter repair and a structural treatment of the empty store before intake. This is the kind of practical, specific outcome expected from every inspection.

lessons.title: Evidence, feedback and professional growth
lessons.html:
Building your evidence

Work experience modules are assessed on evidence that you have performed the work to the required standard in a real workplace. Keep a logbook or portfolio from the start.

What to keep

EvidenceExample
Logbook entriesDate, site type, inspection type, your role, hours
Completed inspection reportsWith client details removed or with permission, according to confidentiality rules
Site plans and checklistsShowing marked findings and device locations
Mentor sign-offConfirmation that you performed the task competently
ReflectionsWhat you learned and what you would do differently

Respect client confidentiality. Do not share photographs or reports outside your company and training provider, and remove identifying information where required.

Learning from feedback

Ask your mentor to review your reports. Common feedback points for new inspectors include missed areas such as roof voids or the backs of equipment, vague findings such as "some rat activity" instead of station numbers and counts, recommendations that do not separate client actions from treatment actions, and reports that fail to list inaccessible areas. Correct these in your next inspections and record the improvement.

Safety habits to show

  • Always signing in and completing inductions.
  • Assessing hazards before entering each area.
  • Refusing to enter confined spaces without permits and standby persons.
  • Wearing the right PPE for the site.

Key points

  • Inspect a variety of real sites, from silos to farms and food factories, under a mentor.
  • Follow the full inspection process from preparation to client briefing and report.
  • Keep a logbook and portfolio of reports, plans and mentor sign-offs.
  • Protect client confidentiality in your evidence.
  • Use mentor feedback to make findings specific and reports complete.
